title: Workplaces thrive when they welcome people with disabilities
summary: Businesses that hire people with developmental disabilities provide those workers a valuable service, writes Robert T. Ireland, but they also help themselves, getting dedicated workers who enrich colleagues, lower turnover and boost customer loyalty.
content:
by Robert Ireland, Maryland Matters December 25, 2025

by Robert Ireland, Maryland Matters December 25, 2025

What does it look like when someone truly loves what they do? Spend a morning with Spike at Royal Farms. For more than six years, he has stocked shelves, organized inventory, cleaned and supported his team in ways that help the whole store run smoothly. His enthusiasm lifts the people around him and quietly shapes the experience of everyone who walks through the door.

Stories like Spike’s are powerful examples of what can happen when businesses open their doors to people with developmental disabilities. Employing individuals with disabilities strengthens the workplace in real and measurable ways. It strengthens our communities as well. Yet far too many people with disabilities still struggle to find meaningful employment.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the unemployment rate for people with disabilities is twice the rate of those without disabilities. Only a quarter of working-age adults with disabilities participates in the labor force, compared with nearly 70% of those without disabilities.

Many people with developmental disabilities want to work but never receive the opportunity. Fewer than 20% have a paid job in an integrated setting, and among those who do not, nearly half say they want one.

Employers play a vital role in closing this gap.

When they embrace the strengths of people with disabilities, the benefits reach far beyond the individual employee. Businesses report that team members with disabilities are dedicated, dependable and eager to contribute. Many employers tell us that welcoming these employees brings renewed purpose to the workplace. Staff morale improves, teamwork deepens and customers notice the difference.

Research supports this experience. A study from the University of Toronto found that businesses that employ people with disabilities see financial benefits, including cost savings from higher retention. They also experience stronger employee and customer loyalty, as well as meaningful improvements in workplace culture.

People with disabilities bring unique perspectives and thoughtful problem solving. When they are part of a team, colleagues often become more mindful of how to make their work environment stronger and more welcoming for everyone.

Creating a supportive workplace for people with developmental disabilities does not need to be complicated. A few guiding practices can make a meaningful impact.

Many local employers have seen firsthand how powerful this can be. Hannah Olexy works at Moonlit Acres Retreat Farm as a peer advocate specialist. She creates workshops and programs for people in the neurodivergent community, from gardening activities to health and safety training. Assistant Director Todd Bonney says, “Not only did we realize she can provide service, but in many ways she is doing it better than we do.” Hannah brings insight, compassion and leadership to everything she does.

Now is the time to make sure our workplaces reflect the belief that everyone has something valuable to offer. Creating employment opportunities for people with disabilities is not only the right thing to do. It strengthens businesses, builds healthier communities, and helps people discover purpose and pride in their work. When we open doors for others, we all move forward together.
